Pema has lived in four cities since I met her, and this year alone she's taken up pottery, Portuguese and a podcast about bridges. At our design firm in Pune, half the team loves her pitches. The other half rolls their eyes: "Another Pema idea, gone by Friday." I used to be in the second half. Then I watched her, in a client meeting, pull a solution out of something she'd learned in pottery class, and nobody else in that room could have made the leap. Still, her half-finished decks pile up. Last month I offered to be her "Friday person": she brings me one idea, and we write three next steps together. Two of them are already live.
Jomon

Peer-mentor note, 12 August. Urmila, same team
Shankar and I became friends the week he joined, eight months ago, from a startup in Kochi; before that, a bakery; before that, a year of teaching in Ladakh. In meetings he throws out three new ideas an hour. Some colleagues find it energising. One told me privately that he is "a flake who won't last the year." I don't agree with either extreme. His idea of reading circles at the bus depot is the best thing we have tried. But his project tracker has six rows marked "started" and none marked "done". Today I asked him to pick one idea to finish before starting any new ones. He chose the bus depot. We will check in each Monday.

passage:
Tuesday night
Chetan told the whole lunch table today that he's moving to Dehradun to start a small coffee roastery. Last year it was Pondicherry and pottery. Before that, a podcast about old maps, three episodes. Suresh rolled his eyes and muttered 'flaky' once Chetan went for more rice. I said nothing, and I've been annoyed with myself all evening. Because Chetan's ideas are the best in our team. He redesigned the returns form in one afternoon; nobody else would have seen that. But I've also watched the pottery wheel gather dust on his balcony. I don't think he's short of ideas. He needs someone to help turn one into a week-by-week plan. Tomorrow I'll ask if he wants to sketch the roastery out properly, step by step. Or maybe that's me being the boring one again.
Naveen

passage: Every time Irawati came back to Wai, she brought a new plan. Two years ago it was goat cheese; last spring, a homestay for city trekkers. This monsoon she stood at the counter of Vaibhav's hardware shop, rain dripping off her umbrella, talking about a lending library for village children. Old Patil kaka, buying nails, snorted. 'Next month she'll want an airport.' Vaibhav laughed with him, then felt uneasy. He had seen the cheese moulds rusting in her mother's shed. He had also seen fifty children at her storytelling afternoon last Diwali, not one of them bored. 'Where would the books go?' he asked. She hadn't thought of that. He pointed to the back room full of old paint tins. 'Sundays only. You keep the register, I keep the key. Six months, then we see.' Irawati stared, then grinned.

qa.q: What does Irawati want to start this monsoon?
qa.a: A lending library for village children.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav feel after laughing along with Patil kaka?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, because he had seen both the rusting cheese moulds and fifty children enjoying her storytelling.

qa.q: Why is Vaibhav's offer likely to help the library last?
qa.a: It adds what Irawati's plans usually lack: a place, a register, a fixed day and a six-month check.

qa.q: Why might Irawati stare before grinning?
qa.a: Irawati is used to jokes about her plans, so a practical offer of space and a trial period probably surprised and delighted her.

grounding: Shows an observer who sees both the gifts and the unfinished plans of a very open friend, while others call her restless, and helps with follow-through.

passage: In the Barcelona design office, Omar, twenty-five, sat next to Ines. In one year she had started a podcast, learned to sail, moved flats twice and pitched eleven new product ideas. Some colleagues rolled their eyes. "Ines and her next big thing." Omar found her exciting to work beside; her ideas were often the freshest in the room. But he'd also noticed that most of them faded after a week. One Friday she showed him three new sketches. Omar said, "These are brilliant. Which one would you want to see finished by June?" Ines paused. "The recycling app." "Then let's break it into steps." They wrote a plan on the whiteboard. Three months later, the app had its first test users.

qa.q: How many new product ideas had Ines pitched in a year?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How does Omar feel about working beside Ines?
qa.a: He finds it exciting and admires her fresh ideas, though he also notices they often fade.

qa.q: How did Omar help Ines turn ideas into follow-through?
qa.a: He asked her to choose one idea to finish by June and helped break it into steps on the whiteboard.

qa.q: How might Ines feel when her app gets its first test users?
qa.a: Ines may feel proud and satisfied, seeing one of her many ideas finally completed.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a very open peer who keeps switching interests, seeing richness where others see flakiness, and helping her follow through.
